newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan businessmen lobby for more Iraq trade.
newsitem.headline: Jordan businessmen lobby for more Iraq trade.

text.p: Jordanian business leaders hosted Iraq's Minister of Trade Mohammed Mehdi Saleh on Sunday to lobby for a share of the business from the U.N. oil-for-food deal.

Officials said Prime Minister Abdul Karim al-Kabariti would meet Saleh in a further attempt to end the strains in political relations since King Hussein turned against Iraqi President Saddam Hussein last year.
Saleh told Jordan's Chamber of Commerce at a lunch in his honour he was flattered by the Jordanian business sentiment that "reflects the strong Iraqi-Jordanian relations that go back a long time."

He was later to join business leaders in a panel discussion to outline Jordan's business prospects under the U.N deal that allows Iraq to sell $2 billion of oil every six months to buy humanitarian needs. Officials said Kabariti might attend.

Businessmen say the government is belatedly trying to ensure Jordan does not lose out to other countries now courting Iraq. They say good ties would help them recoup losses from trade sanctions imposed on Iraq after its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

Jordanian industrialists also are counting on strong business ties, which weathered the political strains, to sell more medicine, vegetable oil and detergents that have been exempt from the U.N. blockade.
"I expect trade to increase and our aim is that it returns to its former levels. Iraq will give us preference," Khaldoun Abu-Hassan, head of Amman Chamber of Industry, told Reuters.

Jordan's businessmen feel vindicated for resisting pressure to curb ties with Baghdad and look to Israel. While echoing widespread disappointment with the benefits of Jordan's 1994 peace treaty with Israel, they say Iraq is Jordan's natural market.
The pro-Iraq business lobby is lobbying for restoration of a $400 million trade protocol they say was cut by half this year under U.S. pressure.
Most of Jordan's industrial exports to Iraq go through the the protocol, under which Jordanian industrial goods are exchanged for Iraqi oil.
"We are for increasing the size of the bilateral protocol to both meet Iraq's needs and allow its spinoff effects on all sectors of the Jordanian economy," Abu Hassan said.

Officials, who were unwilling to consider the matter a few months ago, say a team led by the energy and finance ministers will go to Baghdad soon to discuss extra oil imports that may open the way for lifting the protocol ceiling.
Iraq supplies Jordan with 75,000 barrels per day of crude and oil products, a deal exempt from the U.N. oil embargo on Iraq.
